title: Understanding Dog Behavior. Chapter 2: Your Dog's Baseline
notes: Chapter 2 video. Narration for ch02s01 to ch02s12 is the trainer's doc (Script v4, the 'Chapter 2: Understanding Your Dog's Baseline' section, up to 'END CHAPTER 2 MATERIAL'). The welcome (ch02intro) and plan (ch02plan) narration were drafted for this video and sent to the trainer. Build with LESSON=lesson-ch2.json.

scenes.heading: Understanding Dog Behavior
scenes.visual_concept: Title slide identical to Chapter 1's: 'Understanding Dog Behavior', Tori's headshot in a green ring, the training photo card, name and credentials; the footer tab shows 2. The chapter title is on the narrated chapter card that follows.

beats.say: Hi, I'm Tori Ganino with Calling All Dogs. Welcome back to Understanding Dog Behavior.
beats.show: The title 'Understanding Dog Behavior' as in Chapter 1; the headshot scales in; the name block appears as the name is said; the training photo tilts in.

scenes.heading: Chapter 2: Your Dog's Baseline
scenes.visual_concept: The chapter card (same look as the automatic chapter cards: big light-green 02, 'Chapter 2', the chapter title), now narrated.

beats.say: This is Chapter 2: Your Dog's Baseline.
beats.show: Big '02', the green bar, 'Chapter 2' and the title 'Your Dog's Baseline' slide in.

scenes.heading: Where we're headed
scenes.visual_concept: Three cards across the slide, one per beat, same design as Chapter 1's plan slide: Why it matters, What you'll gain, How we'll get there (three numbered steps). The current card is outlined in green.

beats.say: Have you noticed that your dog can handle something just fine one day, and the next day, the same thing sends them over the edge? There's usually a reason for that.
beats.show: The 'Why it matters' card slides up; rows land as they are said: Fine one day; Over the edge the next; There's a reason.

beats.say: By the end of this chapter, you'll know what can raise or lower your dog's baseline, and what you can do about it.
beats.show: The 'What you'll gain' card slides up with the promise: Know what raises or lowers your dog's baseline, and what you can do about it.

beats.say: Here's how we'll get there. First, what a baseline is. Second, four areas that can raise or lower it. And third, how those factors add up, and how to bring the baseline back down.
beats.show: The 'How we'll get there' card slides up; three numbered steps land on First, Second, third: What a baseline is; Four areas that affect it; How it adds up, and comes down.

scenes.heading: Your Dog's Baseline
scenes.visual_concept: Recap with Chapter 1's bowl and its seven ingredients; 'This chapter: what can be Changed / Managed / Improved' lights word by word; the ingredients pour into an empty glass pot (no water yet); 'First: your dog's baseline'.

beats.say: In the last chapter, we looked at the ingredients that can help shape a dog's behavior.
beats.show: Chapter 1's bowl with its eight ingredients; pill 'Chapter 1: the ingredients'.

beats.say: In this chapter, we're focusing on factors that can be changed, managed, or improved.
beats.show: 'This chapter: what can be Changed / Managed / Improved', each word turning green as it is said.
beats.onscreen: This chapter: what can be changed, managed, or improved

beats.say: So we're going to add those ingredients to a pot.
beats.show: The bowl tips and the ingredients drop into an empty glass pot. Caption: 'Adding the ingredients to the pot'. No water yet.
beats.onscreen: Adding the ingredients to the pot

beats.say: First, we need to talk about your dog's baseline.
beats.show: 'First: your dog's baseline' beside the empty pot (the water comes on the water slide).

scenes.heading: What Is a Baseline?
scenes.visual_concept: A definition card, then a time line: a calm dog badge sits on a green 'starting state' band before an amber 'Something new happens' marker. Then the band rises and falls between levels with up and down arrows: 'Not fixed. It can change.' Round 8: mood is part of the baseline; a fast emotions line over a slowly shifting mood band.

beats.say: When I say baseline, I mean the dog's overall starting state: their starting level of stress and arousal before a trigger appears.
beats.show: Definition card: 'Baseline = the dog's overall starting state before something new happens.' A time line draws; the dog sits on a green band labeled 'Starting state'; an amber bell marker 'Something new happens' drops onto the line to the right.
beats.onscreen: Baseline: the dog's starting level of stress and arousal before a trigger appears.

beats.say: Part of that baseline is the dog's mood.
beats.show: A 'Part of the baseline: mood' pill appears on the starting-state band.

beats.say: And that baseline isn't fixed. It can change.
beats.show: The green band rises and falls between low and high, with arrows; a chip lands: 'Not fixed. It can change.'

scenes.heading: Picture the Baseline as Water
scenes.visual_concept: A cooking pot draws on and fills with water (no heat, no thermometer yet). A ruler beside it marks Lower and Higher. The water drops and rises with the words. A bracket between the waterline and the rim shows the room left for what happens next: small when the water is high, large when it is low. Chapter 1's eight ingredients float in the water in every pot and ride the waterline. Shared pot module video/scenes/c2_pot.js.

beats.say: Picture your dog's baseline as the starting water level in a pot. It represents their overall starting state, including their cumulative mood.
beats.show: The pot draws on and water pours in to a middle level; the label at the waterline: 'Water level = your dog's baseline', then 'including their cumulative mood'.

beats.say: The starting water level doesn't represent stress or arousal in the moment. We'll add that part in a later chapter.
beats.show: A muted pill beside the pot: 'Not shown: stress or arousal in the moment', with an 'In a later chapter' bookmark.
beats.onscreen: Not shown: stress or arousal in the moment

beats.say: The rim represents the limit of what your dog can manage in that situation. Overflow represents an intense response.
beats.show: The rim glows: 'Rim = what your dog can manage'; the water rises past it and spills down the glass: 'Overflow = an intense response'.
beats.onscreen: Rim = what your dog can manage / Overflow = an intense response

beats.say: A lower starting level leaves more room, so your dog may be able to handle more added stress or arousal before an intense response occurs. A higher level leaves less room, so a smaller amount may trigger that response.
beats.show: Low water, the bracket: 'Lower baseline = more room'; a long amber arrow 'Added stress or arousal' raises it and it stays under the rim ('Still under the rim'). Then high water: 'Higher baseline = less room'; a short arrow 'A smaller amount' tips it over.
beats.onscreen: Lower baseline = more room / Higher baseline = less room

beats.say: Our goal is to help your dog start with a lower baseline, giving them more room to handle added stress or arousal before an intense response occurs.
beats.show: The water drops low; 'Goal: a lower baseline' under the pot; the bracket: 'More room to handle stress or arousal'.
beats.onscreen: Goal: a lower baseline / More room to handle stress or arousal

beats.say: We'll come back to why that becomes important when we start adding heat to the pot.
beats.show: A flame bookmark under the bracket: 'We'll add heat in a later chapter'.
beats.onscreen: We'll add heat in a later chapter

scenes.heading: What Can Affect the Water Level?
scenes.visual_concept: The pot at left with up and down arrows by the waterline. Four area cards stack at right, one per area as it is named (Physical Health; Activity, Stimulation & Natural Needs; Emotions & Recovery; Environment, Predictability & Choice). Then all four drip into the pot at once and the water rises. Chapter 1's eight ingredients float in the water in every pot and ride the waterline. Shared pot module video/scenes/c2_pot.js.

beats.say: So, what can raise or lower that water level?
beats.show: The pot slides in at left; up and down arrows pulse by the waterline.
beats.onscreen: What Can Affect the Water Level?

beats.say: We're going to look at four areas: Physical health. Activity, stimulation, and natural needs. Emotions and recovery. And environment, predictability, and choice.
beats.show: Four area cards slide in at right one per area as it is named, each with its icon and colour.
beats.onscreen: Physical Health; Activity, Stimulation & Natural Needs; Emotions & Recovery; Environment, Predictability & Choice

beats.say: Several of these factors may be affecting the dog at the same time.
beats.show: All four cards glow; a drop in each card's colour falls from it into the pot and the water rises.

scenes.heading: Physical Health
scenes.visual_concept: Physical Health. A drawn dog with five factor chips around it (Sleep, Illness or medical changes, Nutrition, Medication effects or changes, Other physical changes). A sleep chart: hours out of 24 for adult dogs, puppies and older dogs. A person with a bad night, getting sick and a skipped meal, and a 'What I can handle' bar that shrinks; the person becomes the dog and the bar shrinks the same way. Ends with the pot: 'Improve them, lower the baseline'.

beats.say: Let's start with the dog's body.
beats.show: Heading with the area badge; the dog draws on at left.

beats.say: Sleep, illness, nutrition, medication changes, and other physical changes can all affect the baseline.
beats.show: Five chips pop around the dog one per word: Sleep, Illness or medical changes, Nutrition, Medication effects or changes, Other physical changes.
beats.onscreen: Sleep · Illness or medical changes · Nutrition · Medication effects or changes · Other physical changes

beats.say: Many adult dogs sleep around 12 to 16 hours in a 24-hour period. Puppies may need as much as 18 to 20 hours, and older dogs often sleep more.
beats.show: Sleep chart on a 24-hour scale: Adult dogs 12 to 16 hours, Puppies 18 to 20 hours, Older dogs the longest bar, ending in an arrow: 'Often more'.

beats.say: Think about yourself after a terrible night of sleep, when you're getting sick, or when you haven't eaten enough healthy food. Things you normally handle without a problem may bother you much more.
beats.show: A person with three small badges (bad night, getting sick, skipped meal) and a 'What you can handle' bar that shrinks.

beats.say: Dogs can experience that same change in tolerance.
beats.show: The person becomes the dog and the bar shrinks the same way.

beats.say: These things don't automatically cause unwanted behaviors, but improving them can help lower the dog's baseline.
beats.show: A small pot appears; the water drops with a green arrow: 'Improve them, lower the baseline'.

scenes.heading: Pain & Discomfort
scenes.visual_concept: Pain & Discomfort. A dog with a faint hidden pain glow that a magnifier finds: 'Pain may not always be obvious.' A person with a headache and four everyday demands (touch, bump, noise, a request). Limping, Crying and Obviously injured chips struck through. The dog surrounded by seven examples (Touch, Movement, Handling, People, Other dogs, Noise, Activity). A sudden-change line and a green vet card. A stoic-dog time line: pain builds long before the limp you notice, unless it is a sudden injury.

beats.say: Pain and discomfort deserve some extra attention because they can be easy to miss.
beats.show: The dog draws on; a magnifier sweeps over it and finds a faint red glow on the hip: 'Pain may not always be obvious.'
beats.onscreen: Pain may not always be obvious.

beats.say: Think about having a headache or back pain. You may still go about your day, but being touched, bumped into, dealing with noise, or even having someone ask something of you may be harder to tolerate.
beats.show: A person with a red pulse at the head; four demand badges arrive one per phrase (touched, bumped into, noise, asked something) and each flashes amber.

beats.say: A dog doesn't have to be limping, crying, or obviously injured for discomfort to affect behavior.
beats.show: Three chips: Limping, Crying, Obviously injured; a red line strikes through each.
beats.onscreen: Not always limping, crying, or injured

beats.say: Dogs can be naturally very stoic. Unless it's a sudden injury, like a broken leg, by the time you see obvious signs like a limp, the dog may have been in pain for quite a while.
beats.show: A time line: a red pain line climbs slowly for a long stretch while the dog looks fine; only at the end does a 'Limp you notice' marker appear; a bracket over the stretch reads 'Already in pain'. A side card: 'Sudden injury (like a broken leg): signs right away'.

beats.say: Pain can change how a dog responds to touch, movement, handling, people, other animals, noise, activity, and everyday events in their environment.
beats.show: The dog at centre; eight example badges pop around it one per word: Touch, Movement, Handling, People, Other animals, Noise, Activity, Everyday events.
beats.onscreen: Touch · Movement · Handling · People · Other animals · Noise · Activity

beats.say: So when behavior changes, especially if the change is sudden or unusual for that dog, pain and other medical concerns should be considered.
beats.show: A behavior line jumps suddenly ('Sudden or unusual change'); a green vet card slides in: 'Consider pain and medical concerns'.

scenes.heading: Activity, Stimulation & Natural Needs
scenes.visual_concept: Activity, Stimulation & Natural Needs. Slider from Too little to Too much; Bored all day and Exhausted cards; a balance beam with the four needs that tips to each side with the doc's examples; then it levels: 'The right balance for this dog', 'More exercise' and 'More enrichment' struck through, and 'More on this later', all on the beam slide.

beats.say: More activity isn't always better, and less activity doesn't always mean a calmer dog.
beats.show: A slider draws from 'Too little' to 'Too much' with a green middle zone; the knob runs right ('More isn't always better'), then left ('Less doesn't always mean calmer').
beats.onscreen: More isn't always better. Less doesn't always mean calmer.

beats.say: Think about the difference between being bored all day and being completely exhausted after an overly busy day.
beats.show: Two person cards at the slider's ends: 'Bored all day' and 'Exhausted'.

beats.say: Neither one necessarily leaves you feeling your best.
beats.show: Both cards fade to amber with a flat face.

beats.say: Dogs need an appropriate balance of physical activity, mental activity, opportunities to engage in natural behaviors, and rest.
beats.show: The slider clears; a balance beam with four weights landing one per phrase: Physical activity, Mental activity, Natural behaviors, Rest; the beam levels.
beats.onscreen: Physical activity · Mental activity · Natural behaviors · Rest

beats.say: A dog who doesn't have enough appropriate outlets may become frustrated or restless. But constantly exercising, entertaining, or stimulating a dog can also interfere with rest and recovery.
beats.show: The beam tips to 'Too little' with 'Frustrated, restless' and the too-little examples; then tips to 'Too much' with 'Overtired, highly activated' and the too-much examples.
beats.onscreen: Too little: frustrated, restless. Too much: gets in the way of rest and recovery.

beats.say: Over time, either extreme can influence the dog's overall baseline.
beats.show: Both columns light up; 'Over time, either extreme affects the baseline'.

beats.say: Think of it like Goldilocks: not too little, not too much, but just right.
beats.show: The examples fade and the beam levels; 'Not too little. Not too much. Just right.' lands under it, the beam glows green.

beats.say: The goal isn't simply more exercise or more enrichment. It's finding the right balance for that individual dog.
beats.show: The columns fade and the beam levels; 'More exercise' and 'More enrichment' are struck through; 'The right balance for this dog' lands under the beam.
beats.onscreen: The right balance for this dog

beats.say: We'll go much more into this later.
beats.show: A 'More on this later' tag on the same slide.

scenes.heading: Emotions, Mood & Recovery
scenes.visual_concept: Emotions, Mood & Recovery. A fast emotions line (fear, frustration, excitement, settling) over a slow mood line; the coworker graph (difficult conversation, the feeling stays, something else happens, a different response); the legend switches to the dog; repeated experiences and too little recovery drip into the pot and the water rises; a quiet event still adds a drop.

beats.say: Emotions are constantly changing.
beats.show: The pot at right; at left a dog in a soft panel: 'Emotions: constantly changing'.

beats.say: A dog may experience fear in one moment, frustration in another, excitement later, and then begin to settle again.
beats.show: A bubble pops up over the dog for each feeling (Fear, Frustration, Excitement, Settling) and fades; the panel's tone shifts a little each time and stays shifted.

beats.say: Those individual emotional experiences can influence the dog's broader mood.
beats.show: 'Mood: the overall tone, shaped by all of these' with a swatch of the panel's colour.

beats.say: Think about having a difficult conversation with a coworker that leaves you upset or frustrated.
beats.show: The coworker graph: a shaded 'Difficult conversation' stretch and the upset line rising.

beats.say: The conversation ends, but the way you feel doesn't necessarily disappear with it.
beats.show: The conversation ends; the line stays high: 'Still upset'.

beats.say: If something else happens shortly afterward, you may respond differently than you normally would.
beats.show: 'Something else happens' under the axis; the line spikes: 'Different response'.

beats.say: Dogs can experience something similar.
beats.show: The legend switches from you to your dog.

beats.say: An unpleasant or stressful emotional experience, even a single one, can affect the dog's overall mood and add to the water level in the pot, especially when those experiences happen repeatedly or there isn't enough opportunity to recover between them.
beats.show: 'An unpleasant or stressful experience' drips into the pot; 'Mood affects whether the water goes up or down'; 'Repeated, or not enough time to recover' adds another drop.
beats.onscreen: An unpleasant or stressful experience · Repeated, or not enough time to recover

beats.say: An experience doesn't have to produce a big, obvious response to have an effect.
beats.show: A calm dog, a small bell: 'No big reaction... still an effect'; one more drop.
beats.onscreen: No big reaction, still an effect

scenes.heading: Environment, Predictability & Choice
scenes.visual_concept: Environment, Predictability & Choice. Three amber cards for the human example (What's next?, Plans keep changing, No say), which turn green (Predictability, Control). A dog badge joins. Then the pot: Changes in routine, Unpredictability, Social conflict, Can't move away, Punishment or confrontational handling, Little control drip in one per phrase and the water rises. Chapter 1's eight ingredients float in the water in every pot and ride the waterline. Shared pot module video/scenes/c2_pot.js.

beats.say: A dog's environment can also affect their baseline.
beats.show: Heading with the area badge; a house icon.

beats.say: Think about how stressful it can be when you don't know what is going to happen next, plans keep changing, or you have very little say in decisions that affect you.
beats.show: Three amber cards one per phrase: 'What's next?', 'Plans keep changing', 'No say'.
beats.onscreen: What's next? Plans keep changing. No say.

beats.say: Having some predictability and control often makes situations easier to handle.
beats.show: The cards flip green: 'Predictability' and 'Control'; 'Easier to handle'.

beats.say: Dogs benefit from that too.
beats.show: A dog badge joins the green cards.

beats.say: Changes in routine, an unpredictable household, social conflict, limited opportunities to move away or opt out, punishment, and having little control over what happens to them can all raise the water level.
beats.show: The cards clear; the pot at right; six red and amber stressor chips drip in one per phrase and the water rises.
beats.onscreen: These can raise the water level

scenes.heading: These Factors Can Add Up
scenes.visual_concept: These Factors Can Add Up. A stack of the day's problems grows beside a person (Slept poorly, Headache, Skipped lunch, Stress at work, Unexpected problem); the last block makes it wobble. Then one pot: Poor sleep, Pain, Too much or too little stimulation, Change at home, Stressful experiences drop in and the water rises step by step to just under the rim. Ends on two pots, same dog: 'Same dog. Different baseline.' Chapter 1's eight ingredients float in the water in every pot and ride the waterline. Shared pot module video/scenes/c2_pot.js.

beats.say: These factors rarely exist in isolation.
beats.show: Heading; a row of small factor dots joins into a cluster.

beats.say: Imagine you slept poorly, have a headache, skipped lunch, had a stressful interaction at work, and then came home to an unexpected problem.
beats.show: Blocks stack up beside a person, one per phrase: Slept poorly, Headache, Skipped lunch, Stress at work, Unexpected problem.

beats.say: That problem might normally be manageable, but on that particular day, your response may be very different.
beats.show: A small 'Normal day' stack with just the problem: 'Manageable'; the tall stack wobbles: 'That day: harder to handle'.
beats.onscreen: Normally manageable. That day: harder to handle.

beats.say: For a dog, it might be poor sleep, pain, too much or too little stimulation, changes at home, or even a single unpleasant or stressful experience.
beats.show: Five red and amber factor pills appear one per phrase; each drips into the pot and the water rises a step (the ingredients ride up with it).
beats.onscreen: Poor sleep · Pain · Too much or too little stimulation · Change at home · Unpleasant experiences

beats.say: Each factor can affect the dog's overall state, and together they can weigh on the dog's mood and raise the water level.
beats.show: Plus signs link the chips; the water reaches just under the rim; the bracket shows 'Little room left'.

beats.say: Same dog. Different baseline.
beats.show: Two pots side by side with the same dog above them: low water and high water. 'Same dog. Different baseline.'

scenes.heading: The Baseline Can Change
scenes.visual_concept: The Baseline Can Change. The full pot (ingredients floating) beside six red and amber factor pills; a magnifier scans them; green checks; one change after another (Tori cut the list sentence) turns a factor into its fix and a drop lifts out of the pot, so the water drops a step. Ends low with a down arrow and 'More room'. Chapter 1's eight ingredients float in the water in every pot and ride the waterline. Shared pot module video/scenes/c2_pot.js.

beats.say: This is why identifying these factors is so important.
beats.show: The full pot and six factor pills; a magnifier scans down the list.

beats.say: Many of them are things we can do something about.
beats.show: A green check pops beside each factor; then, one after another, each factor turns green, a drop lifts out of the pot and the water drops a step (no list read aloud).

beats.say: As we improve these factors, we can lower the water level.
beats.show: The water settles low; a big green down arrow; the bracket stretches: 'More room'.

scenes.heading: The Water Level Is Only Part of the Picture
scenes.visual_concept: The pot (ingredients floating) with three checks; 'Distant antecedents' outlines the water only; a Part 1 (ingredients) and Part 2 (water) frame beside an empty dashed Part 3 frame with three questions; a dashed slot, then a thermometer drops in: Part 3 is temperature. Logo close. Chapter 1's eight ingredients float in the water in every pot and ride the waterline. Shared pot module video/scenes/c2_pot.js. Round 8: the distant antecedents line is no longer narrated; the label stays on screen under Part 2.

beats.say: Now we know what the water level represents.
beats.show: The pot and one check: 'What the water level represents'.
beats.onscreen: We know what the water level represents.

beats.say: It reflects the dog's overall baseline, including their cumulative mood.
beats.show: A dashed outline hugs the water: 'Overall baseline, including cumulative mood'.

beats.say: But the water level doesn't tell us how aroused or stressed the dog is in a particular moment.
beats.show: Part 1 (ingredients) and Part 2 (the water) frame the pot; the empty right half asks 'Arousal and stress in the moment?'.
beats.onscreen: Arousal and stress in the moment?

beats.say: For that, we need to add another part to our pot.
beats.show: A dashed outline appears on the pot where a new part will go.

beats.say: Temperature.
beats.show: A thermometer drops into the pot and its line rises; the second frame becomes 'Part 3: Temperature' with 'Now, how hot is it?'; then the logo close.

beats.say: We'll get to temperature later. First, in the next chapter, we'll step away from the pot and look at the ABCs of behavior.
beats.show: The 'Now, how hot is it?' line clears; 'Next chapter: The ABCs of Behavior' with A, B, C badges; then the logo close.
beats.onscreen: Next chapter: The ABCs of Behavior
